phase1.intro:
Time to actually hire a second worker.

Which way of creating a thread do you want to see first?

topics.buttonText: What are the three ways to hand Java a thread's work?
dialogue: [[key:There are three ways to hand Java a thread's worth of work]]: extend Thread and override `run()`; implement Runnable and pass it to a Thread; or skip the class entirely with a lambda, since Runnable is a functional interface.
[[warn:Runnable is generally preferred over extending Thread]] — Java only allows single inheritance, and Runnable keeps "this is a thread" and "this is the work" as separate ideas.

stickyNote.term: Three Ways to Create a Thread
stickyNote.flavor: 🧵 extend Thread, implement Runnable, or use a lambda
stickyNote.definition: extend Thread + override run(); implement Runnable + pass to a Thread; or a lambda (Runnable is functional). Runnable is generally preferred.

topics.buttonText: What happens if I call run() instead of start()?
dialogue: [[warn:The single most common new mistake here is calling run() instead of start()]] — run() just calls the method directly, on whatever thread called it. [[key:start() is the one that actually asks the JVM to spin up a new thread]] — call run() by accident and it runs sequentially on the main thread, no error, just quietly not-actually-multithreaded.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚫 run() is just a method call, start() spins up a thread
stickyNote.definition: run() executes directly on the calling thread — no new thread. start() actually creates a new thread and runs the work on it.

topics.buttonText: What do setName(), setPriority(), and setDaemon() do?
dialogue: [[fun:A couple of thread properties worth knowing]]: `setName()` gives a thread a readable label, `setPriority()` hints how eagerly the scheduler should favor it, and `setDaemon(true)` marks it as background work the JVM shouldn't wait around for.

stickyNote.flavor: 🏷️ name, priority hint, and daemon status
stickyNote.definition: setName() labels a thread. setPriority() hints (not guarantees) scheduling priority. setDaemon(true) means the JVM can exit without waiting for it.

phase1.openingDialogue: Three ways to create a thread — but the real trap is calling run() when you meant start(). 🧵

phase2.errorMessage:
Thread: main
Thread: main

(No error — but the threads DON'T ACTUALLY RUN IN PARALLEL! They run on the main thread.)
phase2.explanation:
No crash, no error message — [[warn:but this is still a bug]]. The output shows "Thread: main" printed twice, which means both threads ran on the main thread sequentially, not in parallel like intended.

[[key:this happens when run() gets called directly instead of start()]] — run() is just an ordinary method call, executed immediately on whatever thread calls it, with no new thread involved at all. It's the single easiest mistake to make with threads precisely because it doesn't error: the code runs, produces output, and looks like it's probably fine until you notice the threads never actually overlapped.

The fix is one word:

MyThread t1 = new MyThread();
t1.start();  // not t1.run()

start() is what actually asks the JVM to allocate a new thread and hand run() to it — calling run() yourself skips that step entirely.

phase3.openingDialogue: Create threads — start your parallel journey! 🚀

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates 3 threads using Runnable interface
2. Each thread prints numbers 1-5 with a 500ms delay
3. Each thread has a name: "Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"
4. Start all 3 threads

Bonus: Use lambda syntax for one of them.

phase5.trivia: Every Java program already has at least two threads running before your own code creates any — the main thread executing main(), and a garbage collector thread working quietly in the background the whole time.
